topic: Meridian vs Boreal for an internal inventory application
purpose: Help select an operating approach for a small internal app; explain what would change the choice
scope: Deployment, concurrency, maintenance and evidence limits in the supplied synthetic materials only

findings.title: Let instance topology and write contention drive the choice

summary.text: For a single application instance with modest writes, Meridian is a candidate. When several application instances need shared data or concurrent writers, Boreal is a candidate, subject to contention and tuning checks.

implications.text: Check how many application instances must write shared data before choosing an embedded file or a network service.

conditions.text: Meridian shared-filesystem locking requires validation; Boreal concurrent writers can still wait or retry, and its connection and transaction settings need workload-specific tuning.

gaps.text: The application topology, write rate and update-contention pattern were not supplied.

findings.title: Both approaches need explicit recovery and access ownership

summary.text: An embedded database removes the separate service in this comparison, but it does not remove backup or access responsibilities. A separate service adds explicit update, monitoring, access-control and recovery duties.

implications.text: Assign an operator and test a recovery procedure for either option before relying on it.

conditions.text: Meridian open-file copies can be incomplete. Boreal high availability needs additional configuration and the fixture does not promise uninterrupted failover.

gaps.text: Recovery objectives, restore-drill results and maintenance ownership are unknown.

findings.title: The supplied documents establish no throughput or cost winner

summary.text: Neither fixture supplies comparative throughput measurements, and Boreal supplies no operating-cost figures. These materials do not establish a measured performance or cost winner.

implications.text: Validate representative workload behavior before converting concurrency capability into a performance recommendation.

gaps.text: No runtime benchmark, migration, cost study or production validation was performed.

blocks.text: This is a controlled exercise using supplied fictional documentation; it is not guidance for a real database deployment. No network source or workload was tested.

For a single application instance with modest writes, Meridian is a candidate. When several application instances need shared data or concurrent writers, Boreal is a candidate, subject to contention and tuning checks.

sections.title: What the concurrency statements actually allow

blocks.text: Meridian permits one writer per database; readers can continue during a write only when journal mode is enabled. Its documented candidate workload is one application instance with modest writes, and a shared filesystem requires locking validation.

Boreal serves several application instances over the network and supports concurrent writers. Conflicting updates may wait or retry, so this is a capability difference rather than evidence of better throughput for the inventory app. Connection limits and transaction behavior require workload-specific tuning.

sections.title: Recovery and access still need an owner

blocks.text: For Meridian, use its backup interface or stop writes before copying: an open-file copy may be incomplete. Access protection belongs to the application and operating system because no database server is exposed.

For Boreal, configure access control, install supported updates, schedule backups, test restores and monitor the service. Someone must own recovery. A logical export is available; high availability requires extra configuration and does not promise uninterrupted failover in the supplied fixture.
Neither fixture supplies comparative throughput measurements, and Boreal supplies no operating-cost figures. These materials do not establish a measured performance or cost winner.

The missing inputs are actual instance count, conflicting-write behavior, filesystem topology, recovery objectives, restore evidence and operating ownership. Resolve these before making an unconditional recommendation.
